endorsements.quote: If we want to use an AI system in a clinical workflow, its risks need to be assessed and QA measures need to be defined.
We advocate for vendors of a clinical AI system to provide a detailed documentation about the robustness assessment and risk evaluation of their system.
First, we take the view that there is a shared responsibility between the vendors and users when implementing AI system in a clinical workflow.

In analogy to the recurring dosimetric measurements of a QA program in radiation oncology, we believe that setting up a series of periodic in–house and vendor independent tests of the AI system’s performance can provide confidence and trust in the AI model.
This could be e.g. a user-specific test data set that includes adversarial examples, randomly generated data, corrupted or otherwise faulty input.

unlisted_practices: Include a threat model (goals, knowledge, capabilities) in a medical AI device's scope definition and robustness assessment.
Apply the AAPM TG-100 risk-based methodology (process mapping, FMEA, fault tree analysis) to build a quality management program for the whole clinical workflow containing AI.
Assign high risk priority numbers to black-box AI tools when users cannot assess their robustness, and focus mitigation on other steps of the clinical process.
Share the risk evaluations underlying CE marking or FDA approval with AI users.
Design workflow safeguards such as four-eye sign-off and adequate interpretation time so clinicians catch faulty AI outputs.

screen.reason: This paper presents a conceptual framework and methodology based on AAPM Task Group 100 for developing quality management and risk-driven governance for AI systems in clinical workflows.
